The post The Power of Choice in Urban Mobility: Lessons from Delhi’s Clean Transport Transition and Relevance for Niamey appeared first on CPR.
item.content:encoded:
The United Nations defines the “sustainable energy transition” as a structural shift away from fossil fuels toward a system centered on renewable energy. Crucially, the UN emphasises that a truly “just transition” must prioritise equity and inclusion—ensuring that clean energy systems are accessible to all segments of society, leaving no one behind. 

When discussing the transition from fossil fuels to clean energy, international or national policies discussions often focus on massive infrastructure investment or regulations that mandate the change. However, an equal catalyst for the green transition may be simpler than we often assume: the power of choices.

Authors Richar Thaler and Cass Sunstein in their book, Nudge, introduced the concept of ‘Choice Architecture” and ‘Nudge Theory’, argued that people do not make choices randomly rather, the way options are presented within our environment heavily influences the decisions we make. In urban design, a well-designed city ‘nudges’, people towards healthier or more sustainable behaviors, such as walking, cycling, or recycling, by making those choices the default, easiest, most intuitive and most accessible options without restricting individual’s freedom to choose otherwise (Thaler and Sunstein, 2008).

This principle is particularly relevant to urban transport. Populations are more likely to move away from traditional carbon-intensive modes of transportation when cities provide multiple sustainable alternatives that fit into their daily routines, accessibility, travel-time, and cost. Indeed, transitioning from Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) to Electric Vehicle (EV), or to public transport, may not be as simple as policymakers assume, especially if one has to make significant sacrifices. For instance, a commuter may be reluctant to adopt a greener transport option if doing so requires walking a mile from home or work simply to access it.

After spending nearly two months in Delhi during my internship with the Urban Team at the Centre for Policy Research (CPR), I have witnessed this behavioral design principle in practice. Delhi does not just tell commuters to “be sustainable”, it provides a wide range of alternatives. Depending on destination and preferences, I can reduce the emissions associated with my daily commute by taking Delhi Metro, boarding an electric bus, using an electric auto-rickshaw, or completing the last mile on an app-based at times on electric two wheelers. Sustainability is not presented as an obligation; it is increasingly becoming a convenient choice.

While writing this blog from the premises of the CPR, imagine what my transport choices would look like if I were in Niamey, the capital of Niger. As someone who is aware of the growing risk of climate change, particularly for developing countries, I would not have access to the same range of low-emission transport options available in Delhi. This is not because Niger lacks climate ambitions. On the contrary, Niger’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP, 2022) identifies transport as a key sector impacted by climate change and establishes several strategic objectives for mitigation and adaptation. Similarly, the National Transport Strategy (NTS), aligned with the country’s long-term development vision (SDDCI-Niger 2035), seeks to provide transport services that are sustainable and environmentally responsible. Furthermore, Niger’s Renewable Energy Action Plan (PANER) identifies neem oil as a potential energy source while the Sustainable Energy for All (SEforAll) investment prospectus highlights the production and use of liquid and gaseous biofuels for the transport sector.

Although ″Société des transports urbains du Niger‶ (SOTRUNI) remains the main public urban transport operator, the Nigerien government recently took a significant step forward. On May 18 2026, during a Council of Ministers meeting, it adopted two draft decrees establishing the Nigerien Urban Transport Company (SONITU). Beyond the formal public transport system, urban mobility in Niamey relies heavily on the informal transport sector. This includes shared taxi, private minibuses, three-wheelers (primarily used for transporting goods and furniture), and, in some neighborhoods, motorcycle taxi. However, Niamey’s urban transport system remains constrained by limited infrastructure and lack of diverse mobility options. As a result, citizens continue to rely on the conventional combustion-engine vehicles out of necessity rather than preference.

Beyond the availability of diverse transport choices, financial and regulatory incentives can also accelerate the shift from fossil fuels to clean energy. A recent article by Shivam published by Adda24/7 Current Affairs, titled Delhi EV Policy 2.0 Explained: New Rules, Subsidies, Tax Benefits and Petrol Vehicle Deadlines from July 1, 2026, provides an overview of the Delhi Government’s approval of the Delhi EV Policy 2.0, which is scheduled to run from July 1 2026, to March 31 2030. The policy aims to accelerate the adoption of electric vehicles through subsidies, tax exemptions, scrappage incentives, and the gradual phase-out of petrol and compressed natural gas (CNG) vehicles. Backed by an estimated budget of ₹15,000 crore, it seeks to improve Delhi’s air quality, reduce vehicular emissions, and expand EV infrastructure. Among its most attractive measures is a 100% exemption from road tax and registration fees for electric vehicles with an ex-showroom price of up to ₹30 lakh, generating potential savings of ₹1.5 lakh to ₹2 lakh for buyers. Such measures demonstrate how financial incentives can complement consumer choice by making the transition to clean mobility both economically and practically appealing.

Despite these efforts and the various solutions offered to facilitate urban mobility, Delhi continues to face severe air pollution during certain periods of the year. Although electric buses, metro systems, and other low-emission transport options have expanded considerably, significant persistent air quality challenges remain.

According to data from the Government of India’s Decision Support System (DSS), stubble burning can account for 35–45% of Delhi’s air pollution during peak farm-fire periods. Delhi’s air pollution crisis is influenced by both local sources and external factors, highlighting the complexity of air quality management in the National Capital Region (NCR). DSS data reported by Hindustan Times showed that 67.89% of Delhi’s total PM2.5 pollution originated from external sources, while the remaining 32.11% was attributed to sources within the capital. Among local sources, vehicular emissions accounted for the largest share, contributing 16.43% (Gandhiok, 2025).

Addressing transport-related challenges associated with increasing use of private vehicles will be crucial for Delhi’s sustainable development. A continued shift toward private motorization risks exacerbating, deteriorating air quality, increasing energy demand, and raising carbon emissions. Strengthening public transport and promoting low-carbon mobility options will be essential for aligning Delhi’s urban development trajectory with the objectives of Viksit Bharat 2047 and India’s Net Zero 2070 commitment.

Ultimately, Delhi’s experience suggests that the success of a sustainable urban transport transition depends not only on infrastructure investments and environmental regulations, but also on the choices available to citizens. When sustainable options become convenient, affordable, and accessible, people are more likely to adopt them voluntarily. For cities such as Niamey, the challenge may therefore be less about convincing citizens to embrace greener mobility and more about creating the conditions that allow them to choose it in the first place.

Acknowledgment: The author would like to thank Dr. Pushpa Pathak for her valuable guidance and helpful feedback during the preparation of this blog.

(The author is an intern at CPR and MBA Candidate in Sustainable Development and Management at Nalanda University.)

 

The post The Power of Choice in Urban Mobility: Lessons from Delhi’s Clean Transport Transition and Relevance for Niamey appeared first on CPR.

The post The Indus Waters Treaty and the Climate Crisis It Was Never Built For appeared first on CPR.
item.content:encoded:
The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) of 1960 survived three wars and decades of political hostility between India and Pakistan. That record of durability, however, should not be mistaken for relevance to today’s environmental needs.  The basin the Treaty governs is warming. Glaciers are retreating at rates unimaginable to its negotiators. Hydrological patterns are shifting. Yet political discourse surrounding the IWT remains focused almost exclusively on sovereignty, security, and legal disputes, while climate change, the most consequential long-term threat to the basin, is consistently treated as secondary.

Climate-Blind by Design 

The Treaty’s limitations on climate are structural, not incidental. At the time of signing, comprehensive studies on glacier mass balance did not exist. The assumption embedded in negotiations was that the Himalayan glaciers feeding the Indus system were broadly stable, and future changes due to climate variability were not factored into the design.  The result is a framework that was built to allocate fixed water shares between two countries, not to manage a river system undergoing environmental transformation. There are no provisions for periodic review, no adaptive mechanisms, and no formal process for incorporating scientific advances into governance.  The Permanent Indus Commission, the Treaty’s primary cooperative body, is a data-exchange and dispute-management mechanism, never designed for the world the Indus Basin is now entering.

What the Climate Record Shows 

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (2022)  projects, with high confidence, that by the mid-21st century, the Indus, alongside the Amu Darya and Ganges, will face severe water scarcity challenges as climatic variability acts as a stress multiplier across the basin.  Himalayan glaciers currently supply 60 to 70 per cent of the Indus River’s summer flow and are estimated to be losing eight billion tons of ice annually. The World Meteorological Organization’s (WMO) 2024 State of Global Water Resources confirmed that 2024 was the third consecutive year of record glacier mass loss globally.  Projections indicate a water deficit of up to 50 per cent in both countries’ portions of the basin by 2030.  For Pakistan, which depends on the Indus for approximately 96 per cent of its average annual renewable water resources, the implications are particularly acute.  These are not distant projections. They are documented trends occurring within a governance framework that has no mechanism to respond to them. 

How Geopolitics Displaces Climate 

The pattern is consistent. After the Uri attack in 2016, Indian  Prime Minister Narendra Modi asserted that “blood and water cannot flow together.”   After the 2019 Pulwama attack, India proposed diverting the Indus River. In February 2024, Pakistani media and political figures accused India of “water terrorism” over infrastructure projects on the Ravi River. In each episode, climate governance was either absent or invoked instrumentally within existing political arguments. April 2025 marked the most consequential instance. Following the Pahalgam attack, India placed the Treaty in abeyance and suspended the exchange of hydrological data, including flood warnings, river flow measurements, and glacier melt records, and halted the Permanent Indus Commission’s inspections. Pakistan responded by declaring any diversion of its Treaty-allocated water as an act of war. What was suspended was not merely diplomatic cooperation but the data infrastructure both countries need to manage a basin undergoing accelerating climate change. As WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo has observed: “Without data, we risk flying blind.”  In the Indus Basin, that is now the institutional reality. 

A Structural Problem, Not an Isolated One 

The IWT’s climate blindness is not anomalous in South Asia. None of the region’s existing water-sharing arrangements incorporate climate considerations, with the sole exception of a 2023 Bhutan-India flood forecasting scheme. Climate change, however, does not observe bilateral boundaries. Altered monsoon patterns, glacial retreat, and increasing glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) affect entire basins regardless of how their waters are divided on paper. The challenge is compounded by the fact that climate-related risks operate at a basin-wide scale, while water governance in South Asia remains predominantly organised through bilateral arrangements. India’s August 2024 modification notice acknowledged climate-related pressures among its rationales, a notable shift from earlier arguments centred on hydroelectric disputes. Whether this signals a genuine reconceptualisation of climate as a governance priority remains unclear. Although climate considerations have entered the discourse surrounding the IWT they have not yet begun to drive it. 

Conclusion 

The IWT’s survival across six decades is a genuine institutional achievement. The question now is whether that durability can be converted into adaptability. The Indus Basin is warming, its glaciers are retreating, and the 1960 framework was not designed for these conditions. The suspension of hydrological data exchange in 2025 has removed the empirical basis on which any climate-responsive governance would depend. As long as climate change is processed through the categories of geopolitical competition rather than shared environmental governance, the Treaty’s defining challenge will remain unaddressed, and the cost will be borne not by the States negotiating over it, but by the hundreds of millions who depend on the river for their livelihoods. 

 

 

 

The post The Indus Waters Treaty and the Climate Crisis It Was Never Built For appeared first on CPR.

The post “Not Dilli, Not Pindi, No Other Country, Bangladesh Comes First”: Is the BNP Now a Prisoner of Its Own Rhetoric? appeared first on CPR.
item.content:encoded:
The historic 30-year Ganga Water Sharing Treaty is set to expire on 12 December 2026. For the last three decades, the Treaty has operated uninterrupted, despite occasional strains in the diplomatic relationship between the two countries.

Unlike the relatively favourable political context of 1996, in which the Treaty was signed–when the Awami League had just returned to power in Bangladesh, and India’s United Front was keen to strengthen ties with Dhaka, giving both sides strong political incentives to resolve the long-standing dispute—the political circumstances surrounding the upcoming negotiations are now fundamentally different, unfolding in a far more polarised climate.

This shift has been driven largely by the political upheaval in Bangladesh following the collapse of Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League (AL) in late 2024 and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s (BNP) landslide victory in the February 2026 general elections. The return of the BNP has brought a far more nationalist and confrontational tone to water diplomacy, reflected in the party’s rallying cry during the elections: “Not Dilli, Not Pindi, No Other Country, Bangladesh Comes First.”

The party’s February 2026 election manifesto backed this stance by laying out a foreign policy centred on the principle of “Bangladesh Before All.” It also pledged that the new government would take immediate and effective steps to secure Bangladesh’s fair share of water from major transboundary rivers, particularly the Teesta and the Ganga.This aligns with the party’s history of dodging bilateral cooperation with India, specifically by withholding critical river flow data.

To understand this shift in water diplomacy, one must look at the domestic narrative that brought the BNP back to power. For years, the BNP’s core political strategy was built on a relentless accusation: that Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League was systematically “mortgaging” Bangladesh’s sovereign interests to satisfy its upstream neighbour. While sovereignty has long been a central theme in Bangladeshi political rhetoric, with the two major parties repeatedly accusing each other of compromising or “selling out” the country’s interests to India, the historic, though not unprecedented, collapse of the Awami League completely upended this symmetrical tug-of-war. Because the widespread public sentiment turned so fiercely against Sheikh Hasina, her ousting effectively validated the BNP’s long-standing narrative in the eyes of the public.

This deep-seated domestic friction is rooted in a fundamental ideological battle over who truly protects the legacy of the nation. While the 1971 Liberation War was undeniably a fight for absolute state sovereignty led by the Awami League, the two factions interpret the preservation of that independence in radically different ways. AL’s Bengali nationalism viewed sovereignty through the lens of the 1971 war; freedom from Pakistani military hegemony fought in the name of a Bengali cultural identity that it had always shared with India. Hasina’s regime saw friendly ties with New Delhi as a pillar of regional stability, not a “compromise of independence.” On the other side, BNP’s Bangladeshi nationalism viewed sovereignty through the lens of territoriality, defined by those within the borders, not the cultural affinities that lay beyond them. They argued that by becoming too close, too dependent, and too accommodating to New Delhi, the Awami League was slowly surrendering the very independence won in 1971.

Given that Bangladesh shares 54 rivers with India, disputes like Farakka and Ganga water-sharing
become deeply entangled with broader anxieties over dependence, control, and national sovereignty.
This rhetoric is driven by a zero-sum battle for domestic power, where any international water compromise is instantly weaponised by political rivals as a betrayal of national interests. In such a political climate, a middle-ground treaty becomes entirely unpalatable at home.

Now that the BNP has transitioned from opposition to governance under Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, it must also govern within the political expectations created by its own rhetoric in order to maintain domestic legitimacy. As party leaders have repeatedly declared, Bangladesh is “not seeking mercy from India”—they are demanding their “rightful share.”

If talks hit a wall, the BNP is highly likely to pull out its ultimate weapon: internationalising the dispute. India has always insisted on strict bilateralism, preferring to negotiate one-on-one where it holds natural upstream leverage. But during electoral campaigning, Tarique Rahman warned that if India ignores their demands, Bangladesh will take its water rights claims to international organisations.

This is not empty rhetoric; it is a proven BNP strategy. In 1976, party founder Ziaur Rahman raised the Farakka dispute at both the UN General Assembly and the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) summit in Colombo. Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia also used the same playbook: in her address to the UN’s 50th Anniversary session in 1995, directly accusing India of committing human rights violations through its upstream operations at Farakka, claiming the diversion was pushing millions of Bangladeshis toward poverty and destruction.

Recent developments like the approval of the Padma Barrage project, marketed as an alternative to India’s Farakka “death trap”, and the accession to the UNECE Water Convention show that the BNP is actively trying to build a multi-layered defence to survive its own hardline stance. The UNECE Water Convention accession allows Bangladesh to ground its water claims in internationally recognised legal terms, giving its demands a diplomatic legitimacy that goes beyond what bilateral negotiations alone can offer. Neither move resolves the underlying dispute, but both expand the BNP’s room for manoeuvre without requiring it to publicly soften its position.

By spending years turning every water dispute into a test of national sovereignty, the BNP has raised the domestic price of compromise to a point where no workable deal can be sold as anything other than defeat. Sovereignty rhetoric, once a powerful opposition weapon, has become a governing constraint. That said, they are far from passive prisoners—with enough room to act and shape narratives. The infrastructural investments and legal positioning it has pursued since returning to power represent an attempt to build genuine leverage without publicly softening its stance. The Treaty deadline will not just test Bangladesh’s negotiating position, it will also test whether the BNP can distinguish between the promises that win elections and the terms that keep rivers flowing.

 

The post “Not Dilli, Not Pindi, No Other Country, Bangladesh Comes First”: Is the BNP Now a Prisoner of Its Own Rhetoric? appeared first on CPR.

item.description:

The post Why are Indian Elections so Unpredictable? appeared first on CPR.
item.content:encoded:
“Data forces you to think, and how you think about elections in India.”

With these words, Professor Pradeep K. Chhibber invited the audience to go beyond the surface-level explanation of what dictates Indian elections and confront a fundamental question: why are elections in India so unpredictable?

That question brought a packed audience to the Indian International Centre (IIC) on July 15, for a discussion on why nearly a quarter of India’s electorate shifts its vote from one election to the next, and what this reveals about the country’s democratic politics. The discussion challenged conventional assumptions about Indian elections, to deep dive into how village-level electoral volatility and the weak political mobilisation of poorer classes create shifting voting patterns.

Organised by the IIC in collaboration with the Centre for Policy Research, the discussion featured Professor Pradeep K. Chhibber (University of California), Barkha Dutt (Senior Journalist and Founder, MoJo Story), Roshan Kishore (Political Economy and Data Editor, Hindustan Times), and Rahul Verma (Fellow, CPR). Drawing on Chhibber’s forthcoming book, “The Reciprocity Trap: Weak Parties, Elite Networks, and the Marginalization of the Poor in India”, co-authored with Francesca Jensenius (Professor of Political Science, University of Oslo) and village-level election data, national surveys, and extensive fieldwork, the panel explored why Indian elections continue to defy prediction.

While caste, religion, and community remain central to electoral politics, frequent vote swings and shifting party loyalties suggest that identity alone cannot explain voting behaviour.

Data presented by Chhibber shows that India’s electoral volatility. defined “as the net change within the party system resulting from individual vote transfers”, remained remarkably high between 1952 and 2004 compared with many other large democracies. The evidence raises a compelling question: what drives these persistent shifts in voter behaviour?

Electoral Volatility and Political Stronghold

Polling booth data from the 2009–2019 Lok Sabha elections suggests that electoral volatility originates in the “villages” because of two major reasons, which Chhibber attributes to: lack of local political strongholds, and patterns of identity-based political mobilisation.

An analysis of the Election Commission of India’s polling booth data for the 2009 and 2014 Lok Sabha elections reveals an interesting trend. While many villages gave a clear majority of votes to a single party in each election, very few consistently backed the same party over time.

Chhibber argued that this challenges the conventional wisdom that Indian political parties enjoy stable village-level “strongholds”. A party may win a village by a large margin in one election, but that does not mean voters will support it again in the next. The data shows that electoral loyalties at the village level are far more fluid than is often assumed, making genuine long-term party strongholds relatively rare.

The same trend is visible even during the BJP’s sweeping victory in Uttar Pradesh during the 2014 and 2019 Lok Sabha elections. Despite the party’s perceived national dominance, support at the village level remained more volatile indicating that local voting patterns continue to shift from one election to the next.

“And that’s something you need to think about. So even for the case of the BJP in 2014-2019, the same pattern appears — definitely more strongholds, but not as many strongholds as we like to think there are,” Chhibber noted.

As against the popular belief of “geographical strongholds”, Chhibber also challenged the idea that political parties enjoy geographically entrenched support bases. Comparing village-level voting patterns across states such as Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh, he analysed that different political parties dominate neighbouring regions despite their geographic proximity.

While the BJP and the Indian National Congress (INC) dominated most villages in Kutch, parties such as the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD), the Janata Dal (United) (JD(U)), the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) and the Indian Justice Party dominated villages in Uttar Pradesh during the 2009 Lok Sabha elections.

Teasing one to think, he said, “So in other words, there’s very little evidence that parties control nationally that parties control these geographies.”

Drawing on additional data analysis, such as the spatial distribution of BJP votes in Uttar Pradesh between 2014 to 2019, the speaker returned to his central argument on how Indian voting patterns are often based on weak political strongholds at the village level and the persistent disconnect between poor and political parties.


How EV Affects Vote at Village Levels

Chhibber argued that voters in poorer areas are more likely to change their voting preferences from one election to the next.

Drawing on National Election Studies (NES) and CSDS survey data from 1996 to 2024, he found that poorer voters across all major social groups are less likely to be contacted by political parties during election campaigns. As a result, they are more likely to switch parties, vote for smaller parties or NOTA, and are less likely to turn out to vote.

His forthcoming book argues that these patterns are driven not by voters’ preferences, but by political parties’ failure to engage and mobilise poorer communities during elections, leaving them less politically connected and more open to changing their vote.

The question that follows is why is this the case? Why aren’t the poor mobilised? Well, the answers are multifactored.

Local Influencers and Reciprocity Trap 

Indian elections are infamous for their immensity. In order to self-finance large political campaigns, and with limited grassroots infrastructure and vast constituencies to cover, parties increasingly outsource campaign mobilisation to “local influential figures”, who tend to engage only their own caste- and community-based elite networks. As a result, large sections of poorer voters remain outside the reach of party campaigns, making electoral support more fluid and weakening the emergence of durable local strongholds. 

“What this means is a party system based on caste and community identity politics can coexist with vote volatility. When parties mobilise only a part of each caste and community, they’re only mobilising the elites. This is what we call the reciprocity trap,” Chhibber noted.

To break it down, the ‘reciprocity trap’ is what follows when political parties need votes and funds for winning and political gains. Due to their organisational weakness, local candidates rely on local influencers to provide access to both. These local influencers extract resources from parties, gain wealth, status and impunity. These elite networks are class biased. A reciprocity trap locks parties and influentials into this arrangement. In some cases, this deepens ties between parties and influentials. And therefore the under mobilisation of the poor “is a structural equilibrium of Indian politics.”

Reviewing Chhibber’s analysis, Roshan Kishore observed that funding elections requires wealthy intermediaries, reinforcing patronage networks and limiting the state’s ability to address deeper structural problems. Hence, despite ideological differences, major political parties broadly converge in their relationship with capital.

Class, Caste, and Identity over Populism and Welfarism

An important question, however, remained: what role do welfare schemes and populism play?

Drawing on three decades of covering elections, Barkha Dutt asked whether welfare schemes could mobilise poorer voters by bypassing local power networks. “Is a welfare scheme a form of mobilisation that bypasses the local influential network? This has been known to mobilise masses from weaker economic sections,” she observed.

This returned to the book’s central argument that while welfare schemes and populist measures may temporarily strengthen the relationship between political parties and poorer voters, they do not eliminate parties’ dependence on local elites. As a result, class continues to play a significant role in shaping electoral politics.

Kishore argued that class is often masked by talks of identity politics, even though economic interests continue to shape political behaviour in crucial ways. Recognising this changes how we understand Indian democracy. If stronger party organisations are essential to representing poorer citizens, then the relationship between class, political parties and democratic participation deserves nuanced attention.

He emphasised that democracy is not just about elections, but also about how effectively political parties organise and mobilise people. Parties that are better organised at the village levels are more likely to reach, engage and represent a wider section of society, particularly those who are often left out of the political process.
Looking at India’s political history, Kishore noted that class-based politics was once a significant force, as seen in the early success of the Communist Party of India (CPI). Reflecting on its decline, Roshan argued that communist parties struggled because they failed to effectively address caste alongside class. Outside the states of West Bengal and Kerala, he said, their inability to navigate caste politics limited their electoral appeal and contributed to their decline.

The Case for Bengal and Kerala Stand aside

However, the research also establishes that states, such as West Bengal and Kerala, which have greater political outreach to poorer voters, have lower electoral volatility. This suggests that stronger party structures can reduce dependence on local intermediaries and produce more consistency in voting patterns and durable strongholds. Kerala and Bengal continue to hold local-level Panchayat elections, an important avenue to engage poorer voters directly.

Kishore noted, “West Bengal, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu have partisan tribal elections and party mobilisation is the lever. Our survey data shows that this is not because the poor are poor. But the poor, who are contacted and politically included, their attitudes and political behavior indeed changes.”

For Chhibber, the implication is clear: the political exclusion of the poor is not a structural consequence of poverty, but a consequence of how political parties are organised. Where parties invest in grassroots mobilisation, poorer voters are more likely to participate, remain politically engaged and exhibit more stable voting behaviour. 

 

The post Why are Indian Elections so Unpredictable? appeared first on CPR.

The post Six Words and a Sixty-Year Treaty appeared first on CPR.
item.content:encoded:
How ‘blood and water cannot flow together’ became a political and diplomatic doctrine

The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) of 1960 survived three full-scale wars between India and Pakistan—the 1965 war, the 1971 war, and the 1999 Kargil conflict, as well as major diplomatic crises, including the 2001 Indian Parliament attack and the 2008 Mumbai bombings. For over five decades, the Permanent Indus Commission met annually, exchanging hydrological data even when diplomatic communication between the countries was limited. Then, on 27 September 2016, cooperative mechanisms under the IWT were suspended for the first time. The rupture was driven less by hydrology or engineering constraints alone, and more by politics and rhetoric.

Nine days earlier, on 18 September 2016, militants attacked an Indian Army base at Uri in Jammu and Kashmir, resulting in 19 fatalities. The Indian government linked the attack to a Pakistan-based militant group. At a government review meeting in New Delhi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi stated that “blood and water cannot flow together,” linking water cooperation to the broader security environment. On the same day, India announced it would not convene the next annual meeting of the Permanent Indus Commission until Pakistan ended support for cross-border terrorism.

This statement, while metaphorical, altered the relationship between water management and security. It did not threaten abrogation, announce a legal position, or outline immediate action. Its significance lay in signalling that water would henceforth be tied to political and security considerations. Pakistan depends primarily on the three western rivers of the Indus Basin—the Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab—which were allocated to it under the Treaty. India has limited infrastructure to block or divert these rivers. Statements by the Indian Prime Minister Modi and, later, the Indian Union Minister, Nitin Gadkari, referring to stopping water to Pakistan, largely concerned the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej) that India already utilises domestically. Technically, there was no new water to withhold; politically, however, the statements generated concern in Pakistan. Yet the Treaty’s legal architecture provides important constraints on such possibilities, requiring disputes to proceed through established mechanisms involving the Permanent Indus Commission, Neutral Expert review, and arbitration procedures, with the World Bank playing a facilitating role.

Pakistan’s public and political response was immediate. Addressing the National Assembly, Sartaj Aziz, Adviser to the PM Nawaz Sharif on Foreign Affairs, stated that any attempt to revoke the Treaty could be regarded as an “act of war.” This position was subsequently reinforced through a unanimously adopted parliamentary resolution. Pakistani leaders portrayed India’s actions as a potential instrument of water coercion and stressed that any unilateral measures would be challenged legally.

The doctrine quickly became a tool in India’s domestic political arena. Two months after the 2016 meeting, in November 2016, PM Modi, campaigning in Punjab six weeks before state assembly elections, promised that “every drop of this water will be stopped and given to the farmers of Punjab.” The Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) – Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) alliance was in power in Punjab during that time. Though the alliance ultimately lost the election, competing parties adopted similar positions, making water rights a recurring theme in state-level electoral politics. In subsequent years, the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) also maintained that no water from Punjab should be diverted to Haryana. Such statements show how water-related issues increasingly became part of domestic political contestation, extending beyond India-Pakistan relations to inter-state debates within India.

In February 2019, after the Pulwama bombing, Gadkari reiterated that “not a single drop of water will be allowed to go to Pakistan,” signalling resolve amid domestic electoral and public pressure. These statements followed a pattern: a security event occurs, elections approach, and water-related rhetoric intensifies.

Pakistan’s domestic response and counter-rhetoric

Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari issued a direct threat to India after New Delhi suspended the Indus Waters Treaty in response to the Pahalgam terror attack that killed 26 civilians. In a provocative speech at a public rally in Sukkur, Bhutto-Zardari said, “I want to tell India that the Indus is ours and will remain ours. Either our water will flow through it, or their blood will.”

Between 2022 and 2024, as disputes over the Kishanganga and Ratle dams were referred to international arbitration, Pakistani political rhetoric increasingly framed India’s dam construction as a threat to Pakistan’s water security and as a form of water weaponisation.

This mirrored earlier rhetoric in India, where political actors similarly portrayed the other side as an aggressor in order to mobilize domestic political support.19 Pakistan also emphasised legal recourse, stating that any unilateral action violates the Treaty and is subject to international adjudication.

Cumulative effects of rhetoric

By 2025, after a militant attack in Pahalgam, India effectively placed the Treaty in abeyance, echoing the original 2016 phrasing: “terror and talks cannot happen; water and blood cannot flow together.” Pakistan responded that this constituted an “act of war,” constrained by the prior unanimous parliamentary resolution.

The significance of this development lay not only in its immediate impact on India-Pakistan relations, but also in the broader questions it raised about the future of the Treaty. As political rhetoric increasingly translated into policy decisions, concerns emerged regarding the consequences of such a shift, extending beyond the bilateral relationship to the future of the Treaty itself.

Commentators interpreted this shift in different ways. Former diplomat Syed Akbaruddin argued that the Treaty’s durability should be viewed in the context of India’s long record of upholding it despite wars, terrorist attacks, and prolonged political tensions. From this perspective, the growing linkage between water cooperation and security reflected accumulated frustrations that had become increasingly difficult to separate from the Treaty’s operation. Regardless of interpretation, repeated rhetorical signalling on both sides contributed to a political environment in which compromise became increasingly difficult.

Conclusion

The significance of “blood and water cannot flow together” lies not in the statement itself, but in what followed. Invoked after the Uri attack and recurring after Pulwama and Pahalgam, each a distinct act of cross-border terrorism, the phrase evolved from a crisis response into a recurring reference point in India-Pakistan relations, gathering weight with each repetition rather than fading after the crisis that produced it. Similar rhetoric later emerged in Pakistan, indicating how water increasingly came to occupy a more prominent place in political and diplomatic contestation, with each side’s language reinforcing the other’s over time. As this rhetoric becomes more embedded on both sides, it raises a structural question for the Treaty’s future: whether the technical, depoliticised cooperation that sustained it for over six decades can be restored once water has been so closely tied to security in the public discourse.

item.title: Trade, an Increasingly Important Pillar in Dhampur’s Economy
item.dc:creator: cpradmin
item.description:

The post Trade, an Increasingly Important Pillar in Dhampur’s Economy appeared first on CPR.
item.content:encoded:
In the ancient times, trade was the primary economic activity which led to the establishment of urban settlements, where agricultural surplus was exchanged for manufactured or imported goods like  iron, stone, wood, agricultural implements, textiles, spices, etc. Over time these small market-towns also became industrial centers where artisans and crafts persons produced a range of goods catering to the demands of the towns’ inhabitants, nearby villages as well as for exporting to other regions. Hence, trade and industries became the two main pillars of growth of market towns into larger complex urban centers with multiple functions. Merchants and industrialists have played an important role in the small towns’ development and administration for a long time.


Dhampur, located in the agriculturally rich Western Uttar Pradesh, is an apt example of small towns’ economy where trade and industry have played an equally important role in its earlier development. However, trade seems to be gaining more prominence in the recent decades. The Census of India data indicates that employment in trade in Dhampur increased from about 22 percent in 1961 to 32 per cent in 1991 while employment in both Household and Non-household industries declined from about 26 per cent to 20 per cent in the same years. These two sectors together continue to account for about half of the economic employment of the town. However, the nature of the trade has changed over time both in terms of the nature and quantum of commodities traded as well as the spatial distribution of the trading establishments.

In the late 1970s and early 1980s, the trading area of Dhampur lay along a narrow street in the congested center of the town, where wholesale and retail activities were tightly packed surrounded by densely populated old residential areas. Dhampur had already become one of the district’s main market centers. The Badi Mandi was the center of wholesale trade, with about fifty shops and agencies dealing with sugar export and food grain imports. The retail trade was conducted through around two hundred shops in the Kalan bazar, the town’s main market. Other shops and services were scattered all over the town. A street off the main bazar called Lohiyan was exclusively inhabited by ironware manufacturers and dealers. The bulk of Dhampur’s exports consisted of sugar, handloom cloth and milled rice, while major imports were mill-woven cloth, machinery, food grains, metals, minerals, cotton yarn, and consumer and luxury goods. Farmers did not have good storage facilities in the villages and most agricultural commodities were sold soon after harvesting. Grain traders and agents of rice mills went to the villages to buy grain at the time of harvest. Only a few large farmers took their surplus produce to the nearest grain mandis located at Dhampur or Nagina towns.

Grain trading has also undergone significant shifts. Sugarcane has been the main crop in the region since the 1930s when the earliest sugar mills were established. Comparing recent years to the late 1970s, the price of sugarcane has increased significantly, which encourages farmers to cultivate more sugarcane. As a result, there is a huge decline in the food grain production. Farmers now grow small portions of food grains like wheat and paddy for their self-consumption. Only about 1 per cent of their output of these grains is sold directly in the Dhampur’s Badi Mandi.  Consequently, grain traders are now purchasing branded packed grain and other food products like flour directly from factories in other parts of Uttar Pradesh and other states of India. Alongside this shift, technological changes have also taken place. There are now Japanese grain cleaning machines that remove small pieces of stones from the grain. Firms like Chote Lal Rajeev Kumar Jain, established in 1978, run a wholesale business of food grains. They purchase grains mostly from factories located in Delhi, Saharanpur, Bijnor and Gajraula. About 50 per cent of their buyers are from Dhampur town and 50 per cent from the tehsil.

At present, Dhampur’s trade has multiplied manifold making it a major trading center in the district. Serving around five hundred nearby villages and towns, Dhampur now deals with multiple trade activities from agricultural products to metal, fabric, electronic goods, and a number of consumer goods. There are around fifteen markets and approximately two thousand shops with mixed trade activities. The historic core of the town has become even denser and continues to be the main center of trade. However, there are examples of spatial dispersal of some of the trading activities towards the periphery of the town with wider roads where trucks can turn and unload easily. For example, the vegetable and fruit trade has shifted out from the Badi Mandi in the core town to the New Sabji Mandi on Nehtaur road in the west of the town. It is established on private land taken on lease from the farmers. It is spread over 6.25 acres and has 55 shops of similar size with wide streets that allow trucks to enter. The Nai Sabji Mandi and Fal Association manages the Mandi and also collects a monthly rent from the traders. A similar Sabji and Fal Mandi has come up adjacent to the Nai Mandi, which indicates a complete shift of the fruit and vegetable wholesale market from the core town. The traders purchase fresh fruits and vegetables from Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Delhi and they sell their products to wholesalers who come from different parts of district Bijnor. The Badi Mandi continues dealing with grain trade specializing now in packed grains and other food products. The Lohiyan market is still inhabited by ironware manufacturers and dealers, where people especially from hilly areas come to buy metal-made products such as kadhai and tawa. The outer areas of the town have also seen the emergence of new kinds of trades such as dealing with branded clothing, footwear, televisions, cars, two-wheelers, tractors, medicines and other consumer goods.

 

The major transformation in trade is visible in the import of automobiles and two wheelers. Multiple automobile showrooms have come up in Dhampur. For example, Shakumbari Automobiles, a Maruti Suzuki showroom opened in 2016, imports cars from different states of India including Haryana and Gujarat. Every year, in the lean season it sells about 20-25 cars, and in the peak season sales rise to 30-40. Around 60 per cent of the buyers are from Dhampur town and 40 per cent from Dhampur tehsil. Many cars are purchased by farmers for their daughters’ marriages, where gifting a vehicle has become a symbol of status. Only a small minority of 4-5 per cent buy cars without any social occasion. The showroom now faces competition from other automobile brands, which shows that Dhampur’s demand has risen and people prefer to have a choice.

The textile trade has also transformed remarkably over the past five decades. Now there are fewer shops selling cloth and many more shops have come up selling readymade garments for men, women and children. One such shop is Leela Shadi and Suits, established in 2015, which has transformed from a small-scale to a large-scale firm. About 80 per cent of their dresses are purchased from Surat and Ahmedabad, while the rest 20 per cent comes from Delhi. Around 80 per cent of the buyers are from Dhampur town, 10 per cent are from Dhampur tehsil, and the remaining 10 per cent come from other parts of the district such as Seohara, Nagina, Noorpur and nearby villages. Most of their customers come for the purchase of clothes for marriage purposes. After Covid, their regular customers declined due to shopping from online platforms.

The journey from the congested central street of 1979-80 to the multi-layered trade network of 2023-24 is a story not just of economic change but also of how a small town redefines what it means to live and do business in the present subaltern urban India. Dhampur continues to serve as a vital market center for its rural hinterland and other nearby small towns now plugged into a wider network of trade, industry, technology and developmental aspirations.

Through his leadership, he helped establish […]

The post IN MEMORIAM: Dr Subhash C. Kashyap (1929 – 2026) appeared first on CPR.
item.content:encoded:
We condole the passing of Dr Subhash C. Kashyap, who served as the Honorary Research Professor at the Centre for Policy Research from 1990-2023.

One of India’s foremost constitutional scholars, Dr Kashyap played a pivotal role in shaping public understanding of the Constitution, parliamentary institutions, and democratic governance. Through his leadership, he helped establish and direct several institutions in this field such as the Academy of Grassroots Studies and Research of India (AGRASRI).

A distinguished administrator, Dr Kashyap served the Parliament of India from 1953 to 1990, retiring as Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha. Among his many contributions, he also served on the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution and Chairman of its Drafting and Editorial Committee, led the Inter-Parliamentary Union’s International Centre for Parliamentary Documentation in Geneva till 1983, and advised the Government of India on Panchayati Raj laws and institutions.
A prolific author and respected public intellectual, he was awarded the Padma Bhushan, India’s third-highest civilian honour, in 2015.

As a member of the CPR community, Dr Kashyap enriched public discourse through his intellectual rigour and unwavering commitment to constitutional values. Many fondly remember his contributions to the faculty meetings, where his wisdom and deep engagement with questions of governance and institutional reform inspired colleagues, researchers, and policymakers alike.

The CPR community, its Governing Board, President, faculty, and staff pay tribute to the memory of a remarkable scholar and public intellectual whose work leaves an enduring legacy.
We extend our sincere condolences to his family, friends, and loved ones and join them in this time of grief.

The post Bridging Research and Education to Address Capacity Gaps for Realising Adequate Housing for All appeared first on CPR.
item.content:encoded:
World Urban Forum 13, Baku, Azerbaijan, 21 May 2026

The UN-Habitat Academia and Research Roundtable at the 13th World Urban Forum (WUF13) brought together global experts to confront a stark reality: how the global housing crisis is not just a shortage of buildings, but a profound mismatch of data, capacity, and outdated educational models. The Roundtable was organised in two panels; Panel 1 on research and Panel 2 on academia. I was invited to participate in Panel 1 of the Roundtable as a representative from the Asia Region.

Conceptualised and coordinated by Ms Raphaelle Vignol, Programme Officer, Capacity Development Section, Global Knowledge and Advocacy Division, UN-Habitat, Nairobi, Kenya and moderated by Prof. Carlos Moreno, Sorbonne University, Paris, France, the discussion pivoted away from traditional metrics of “supply and demand” toward a more nuanced, “situated” understanding of how people actually live.

Panel 1: A New Philosophy for Housing Research

In her opening remarks, Ms Ana Claudia Rossbach, Executive Director, UN-HABITAT, highlighted the challenge of a mismatch that exists between the global housing crisis and capacity. There are critical data and research gaps on housing and housing markets in the global South with some communities and geographies suffering much more than others and of course, the capacities are also uneven. While innovation is happening daily on the front lines in the Global South, this knowledge is often “locked” or uncaptured because traditional research is designed around available data rather than ground-level needs.

Referring to the UN-HABITAT Strategic Plan – 2026-29 that puts housing at the centre, along with land, basic services, informal settlements, requires means of implementations, including financial means, urban planning to multi-level governance, the local action, participation, data, access to data, access to knowledge. That’s why it is so important for us to maximise the potential that we have at WUF13, and specifically the WUF Academy, to make sure that we build a community which remains united towards a shared research and capacity development agenda. To this, Ms Ana argued that we must move toward co-production of knowledge where researchers work alongside practitioners and communities who do not have the luxury of time to stop and document their innovations.

Moving Beyond “Units” and “Deficits”

Dr Camila Cociña, Senior researcher (housing justice), International Institute of Environment and Development, presented an unconventional argument that the housing crisis cannot be solved by simply building more houses. and the real gap lies in improving existing housing stock and supporting the efforts people who are making house themselves. This requires researchers to move away from “supply/demand” deficit models and instead understand the “trade-offs” residents make between long-term investment and immediate tenure security.

The Paradox of the “Empty City”

Citing a peculiar phenomenon in the Sub-Saharan Africa, Dr Uchendu Eugene Chigbu, University of Science and Technology, Namibia, highlighted how the presence of high-end, “beautiful houses” in major cities like Lagos and Nairobi remain completely unoccupied while millions suffer from homelessness. He noted that a newly elected government in Ethiopia identified around 200 such unoccupied houses, underscoring the disconnect between housing supply and housing need. He argued that current research relies too heavily on formal market assumption, namely, that that people have titles and access to bank funding. This framework, arguably, fails to capture the data and address the reality of a mobile population of itinerant labourers who move frequently for work and often remain invisible to conventional planning and tracking systems.

Plurality and Changing Minds

Dr David Dodman, General Director Institute for Housing Studies, Netherlands, argued that the “highest goal” of research is not just data generation, but changing minds and actions. He advocated for a plurality of approaches, recognising that no single method —whether it’s mortgages, self-builds, or large-scale public housing — can solve the crisis alone. Highlighting the value of long-term evidence, he pointed to the “longitudinal work” of Caroline Moser as a gold standard for housing research. By tracing how settlements and communities evolve over decades, such research offers perspectives often lost in short-term policy cycles.

The “Invisible” Rental Market

As part of the distinguished panel, I, Dr Pushpa Pathak, Centre for Policy Research, New Delhi, India, drew attention to the massive research gap in the low-income rental housing market. Most housing data focuses on ownership, rental housing remains understudied, at all levels, and especially in informal settlements. This is important because the quality and affordability of rental housing determine the decision to move with family or alone that affects the pace of urbanization, the commitment of people to cities and the nature of rental housing demand. Emphasis should be on understanding the private response to rental housing for lower income groups: who makes it, how is it financed, who does it cater to, and is there discrimination? What are the identity markers of discrimination? Language, religion, region, gender, or family versus single rentals? These questions require deeper empirical investigation to understand rental housing market for lower income groups in Asia’s expanding urban areas.

Big Data vs. Small Data

Dr Karen Chapple, Director of the School of Cities, University of Toronto, Canada, warned of a dangerous trend: while “Big Data” and AI are flourishing, the census and “small data” (household-level surveys) are disappearing or becoming irregular. She shared an unconventional finding from her work at the Urban Displacement Project – on how most people actually experience “emplacement” rather than displacement, implying they try to stay as close to home as possible even under pressure. Without “small data” to understand motivations and choices, Big Data risks making lower-income and racialized populations even more invisible.

The Scale of the Neighbourhood and the City

Dr Margarita Greene, Professor, School of Architecture, Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, argued that research has focused too much on “the house” and not enough on the neighbourhood scale. She suggested that “situated research” is needed to understand how different cultures approach social cohesion. A major failure of modern urbanism, according to Greene, is the inability to “combine properly” different social groups; we need to understand how the poor and the rich can coexist in a way that enriches both rather than leads to segregation.

“Situated” Approach for Reconstruction and Development

Dr Fariz Ismayilzada, Member of Parliament and Vice Director, Azerbaijan Diplomatic Academy (ADA) and Information Technologies University, Baku, Azerbaijan, provided a concrete example of this “situated” approach through the reconstruction of the Karabakh region. He described using university surveys to ensure that the creation of new villages from scratch matched the economic skills and family structures of the 80,000 displaced people returning to their lands.

Panel 2: Higher Professional Education to Fill the Capacity Gaps and Foster Innovation

The second half of the roundtable focused on reforming education to teach the next generation of urban professionals for a world that is changing rapidly.

Housing as Land Policy

Dr Enrique R. Silva, Chief program officer, Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, Cambridge, USA, emphasised that the most urgent gap in education is the failure to link housing policy to land policy. Housing is too often treated as a construction or finance issue when it is fundamentally a land problem. Unconventionally, Silva suggested how land policy literacy at the primary or high school level, can help build a “talent pipeline” of citizens who are aware of their communities and understand how they function.

Universities without Walls

Dr Gul Sola Mamedova, Rector of the Azerbaijan Nature and Construction University, BAKU, Azerbaijan advocated for universities to go “beyond their own walls” and become “city laboratories”. Mamedova emphasised lifelong learning, noting that because cities change so fast, a bachelor’s degree is no longer sufficient; professionals need “agile” programs to upgrade their knowledge on issues like climate change and digitalisation every few years.

The Systems Integrator

Dr.Edgar Pieterse, Founding Director of the African Centre for Cities, University of Cape Town, South Africa, South Africa, emphasised that given the multidimensional nature of sustainable urbanism, housing and the land question, we have to adopt a systems perspective. What is needed are “Systems Integrators” who may start as architects or engineers but are trained to “curate” the process of learning, failing and testing repeatedly within a highly politicised, under-resourced environments. Pieterse argued that these professionals need more than just technical skills; they need “adaptive leadership,”  “spiritual attentiveness” (or “Zen”) and new competencies like AI to navigate the emotional and ethical trade-offs of urban governance. 

The Missing Skill: Urban Finance

Ms Lucy Slack, Commonwealth Local Government Forum, London, UK, pointed out that while we talk about planning, urban finance is rarely treated as its own specialised profession or skill set. She noted that high-level skills often reside in the private sector rather than the municipalities that need them. She called for a “professionalisation of local governments” to make cities places where high-level experts actually want to work.

Professionals as Trans-discipline Bridges

Ms Alexa Martinez Soto, Monterrey Institute of Technology and Higher Education, Mexico, framed housing as a “socio-technical complex system”. She argued that the new generation of professionals must act as “bridges” who can speak the languages of economists, architects, and community members simultaneously. She highlighted the need for “caring cities,” a concept often ignored in technical planning, which focuses on the needs of women and caregivers. Interestingly, she suggested that AI could be a tool for radical inclusion, helping city governments process the “complexity of multiple perspectives” from citizen voice notes and texts that are currently ignored.

City and Housing as Interdisciplinary Conversations

Ms Karla Planter Perez, Rector General of the Universidad of Guadalajara, Mexico, delivered a provocative critique, stating that universities are currently providing “professional training for a world that doesn’t exist anymore”. She argued that because reality is not “segmented,” education must move toward systemic and critical thinking that allows professionals to read “what does not appear on indicators,” such as daily experiences of exclusion. The interdisciplinary vision needs to go beyond infrastructure, finance, and urban planning, and think of the questions around the city and housing as interdisciplinary conversations.

Key Themes Emerging from the Discussions

Several discussions challenged conventional approaches to housing and urban planning, highlighting the need to rethink how cities respond to rapid urbanisation, inequality, and social change.

Focus on Improvement, Not Just Construction
Scholars and experts argued that addressing the housing crisis requires more than increasing housing supply. Equal attention must be paid to improving existing stock and supporting ground-level efforts than by just building new supply.

The Mobile Urban Population Problem
A recurring theme was the growing disconnect between planning frameworks and lived realities. Planners continue to design for static populations while African urban residents are increasingly mobile and “itinerant,” and require entirely new tracking and planning models. Understanding and responding to this mobility remains a significant challenge for housing policy and urban governance.

The “Luxury Vacancy” Paradox
Speakers highlighted the contradiction of rising homelessness existing alongside increasing vacant luxury housing. This phenomenon raises important questions about how housing markets function and whom they ultimately serve, a gap that traditional market research has failed to address.

Emplacement over Displacement
Discussions also challenged assumptions about mobility and relocation. Contrary to common belief, data shows people have a powerful “emplacement” drive, often staying in high-risk or inadequate housing just to remain near their community owing to strong social, economic, and cultural ties Housing solutions, therefore, must account for people’s attachment to place rather than focusing solely on physical relocation.

The Death of the Specialist
As urban challenges become increasingly interconnected, participants stressed the need for professionals who can work across disciplines. The “hyper-specialised” professional (just an architect or just an economist) is becoming obsolete, replaced by “Systems Integrators” who are capable of understanding “interdependencies” of the city.

Spiritual Leadership in Planning
Several speakers reflected on the qualities needed to lead cities through sensitive transitions. Effective urban leadership requires “emotional confidence” and “spiritual attentiveness” to survive the “political fights” of municipal governance.

AI as a Listener
The potential of artificial intelligence was discussed not only as a tool for data analysis but also as a means of engaging with citizen voices at scale. Participants explored how rather than just using AI for data analytics, it can be used to “hear” and process thousands of diverse citizen voices that traditional governments find too “complex” to manage.

In Conclusion: Research and Education for Change

The roundtable concluded with a call for international collaboration to break out of “insular conversations”. As Ms. Raphaelle Vignol summarised, together with you we are going to drive the housing research and capacity development agenda in the next three years. The goal is to move toward research and education that is designed for change, putting the human experience and the “neighbourhood scale” back at the heart of the global housing agenda.

My own personal takeaway is largely similar to Ms. Vignol’s. The thrust of the research panel was to re-scale away from individual housing to neighbourhood level issues and its interaction with housing choices, a greater focus on private responses, especially at lower income groups, which would include rentals and incremental interventions. Similarly, on the educational front, the emphasis was on an approach that equipped students with a more integrated and cross-disciplinary toolkit that could relate to community experiences, rather than specific disciplinary inquiries.

item.content:encoded:
Water is not just a resource; it is also the confluence of political and ecological realities. At CPR, this has been central to our interdisciplinary work on river basin management, interstate cooperation, the politics of infrastructure, federalism, and long-term water security. Our continued engagement with questions of India’s water policy spans decades, with stalwarts like Ramaswamy R. Iyer, B. G. Verghese and R. Rangachari informing the discourse in the past. Through the TREADS Initiative, we further this work by rethinking river water management and its systemic underpinnings for a more equitable water governance infrastructure. These concerns remain intricately connected to how we imagine our shared future.

This World Water Day, we are reminded of why our work remains crucial. Revisit some of the work by CPR’s faculty and researchers on India’s water ecologies, governance and security.

Find more of our work on water here.

Why Do Interstate Water Disputes Emerge and Recur?

This monograph uses the Krishna river dispute as a case study to argue that India’s interstate water conflicts stem from set of legal ambiguities, political antagonisms and physical asymmetries calling for interstate cooperation rather than purely legal solutions. Read here

 

 

Water and Federalism

The study identifies federal consensus-building about the Centre’s role and autonomous institutional architecture for data as the two foundational pillars and makes concrete recommendations to improve federal governance for long-term development and water security. Read here

 

 

The Right to Water, Law and Municipal Practice: Case Studies from India

Recognition of the right to water in Indian courts has had little impact on the ground. This paper explores the disjuncture between what happens in the court and the everyday reality of living with a less-than-perfect claim on city water services in India’s urban slums. Read here

 

 

 

The Evolution of the Right to Water in India

The paper reviews the articulation of the “right to water” in India to show that this articulation has largely been oblivious to the international human rights movement on water. Beyond the mainstream articulation of the “right to water”, the paper describes the specific articulation of the right by two marginalised groups, namely the Dalits and Adivasis. Read here

 

The Decentered Construction of Global Rights: Lessons from the Human Rights to Water and Sanitation

The global right to water is constructed out of the myriad struggles and claims of people experiencing the lack of something essential to a dignified existence, and who cannot obtain an adequate response from their immediate political and legal environment. Read here

 

 

Flows and Flaws: Diverting the Debate on Water with China

Can we frame the water debate with China in ways that can create institutional entry points for a whole set of missing issues that are currently invisible to the mainstream policy and research gaze? Read here

 

 

 

Conserving Freshwater Ecosystems in India: A Call to Action

This paper calls for an urgent and greater focus on implementing conservation actions for freshwater ecosystems in India and suggests a strategy to enhance focus on their conservation. Read here

 

 

Convenience over Control: Qualitative Insights from Water System Users in a Rural Setting in Gujarat, India.

This study suggests that piped water system designs should enable operational flexibility, tailored to community needs, so that water is available when needed. Read here

 

 

Disputes, (de)Politicization and Democracy: Interstate Water Disputes in India

The aleatory nature of politics reshapes the nature and extent of a dispute and contributes to its frequent recurrence. Discourses of policy and governance reforms usually do not account for this contingent nature of politics. Read here

 

 

Water Disputes and the Environment: Transboundary Dimensions

This chapter analyses India’s transboundary water relationships, arguing that despite its hydrohegemonic tendencies and preference for bilateralism; shared environmental risks in South Asia create an opportunity to build regional institutions, starting with disaster resilience as a foundation for cooperation. Read here

 

 

The Human Right to Water in Rural India – Promises and Challenges

India has made remarkable progress in rural drinking water access, rising from 18 percent coverage in 1974 to at least 72 percent today. While this reflects significant advancement in realising the human right to water, full and universal access remains an ongoing challenge. Read here

 

 

The Right to Water in Rural India and Drinking Water Policy Reforms

This chapter uncovers the role played by the state in providing significant resources,like water, to all in rural India. It further analyses the changes that have taken place and the gaps that have arisen in terms of aligning the policy framework with the human right to water. Read here

 

 

Whither India’s Federal Governance for Long-Term Water Security?

The discourse about federal governance is generally dominated by that of fiscal federalism. This chapter takes a closer look at the historical changes in budgetary allocations of the Centre and select states for water resources governance, and argues that federal water governance in India is weakly structured to pursue its development and sustainability goals. Read here

 

 

Shifting Scales from International to Subnational: A Comparative Analysis of India and Germany’s Federal Water Governance

This paper examines the River Basin Management trajectory of Germany vis-à-vis India through a comparative lens. It argues for acknowledging structural differences to enable meaningful knowledge exchanges and  collaborations at the sub-national scale. Read here

 

 

Unravelling Rural India’s enduring water indigence: framing the questions, issues, options and opportunities

The paper extensively reviews India’s centrally sponsored programme for improving drinking water supply coverage in rural settlements. Read here

 

 

India should take a leaf out of Singapore’s water harvesting to solve its crisis

How have India’s collaborative arrangements with Singapore fared? Read here

Water is not just a resource; it is also the confluence of political and ecological realities. At CPR, this has been central to our interdisciplinary work on river basin management, interstate cooperation, the politics of infrastructure, federalism, and long-term water security. Our continued engagement with questions of India’s water policy spans decades, with stalwarts like Ramaswamy R. Iyer, B. G. Verghese and R. Rangachari informing the discourse in the past. Through the TREADS Initiative, we further this work by rethinking river water management and its systemic underpinnings for a more equitable water governance infrastructure. These concerns remain intricately connected to how we imagine our shared future.

This World Water Day, we are reminded of why our work remains crucial. Revisit some of the work by CPR’s faculty and researchers on India’s water ecologies, governance and security.

Find more of our work on water here.

Why Do Interstate Water Disputes Emerge and Recur?

This monograph uses the Krishna river dispute as a case study to argue that India’s interstate water conflicts stem from set of legal ambiguities, political antagonisms and physical asymmetries calling for interstate cooperation rather than purely legal solutions. Read here
Water and Federalism

The study identifies federal consensus-building about the Centre’s role and autonomous institutional architecture for data as the two foundational pillars and makes concrete recommendations to improve federal governance for long-term development and water security. Read here

The Right to Water, Law and Municipal Practice: Case Studies from India

Recognition of the right to water in Indian courts has had little impact on the ground. This paper explores the disjuncture between what happens in the court and the everyday reality of living with a less-than-perfect claim on city water services in India’s urban slums. Read here

The Evolution of the Right to Water in India

The paper reviews the articulation of the “right to water” in India to show that this articulation has largely been oblivious to the international human rights movement on water. Beyond the mainstream articulation of the “right to water”, the paper describes the specific articulation of the right by two marginalised groups, namely the Dalits and Adivasis. Read here
The Decentered Construction of Global Rights: Lessons from the Human Rights to Water and Sanitation

The global right to water is constructed out of the myriad struggles and claims of people experiencing the lack of something essential to a dignified existence, and who cannot obtain an adequate response from their immediate political and legal environment. Read here

Flows and Flaws: Diverting the Debate on Water with China

Can we frame the water debate with China in ways that can create institutional entry points for a whole set of missing issues that are currently invisible to the mainstream policy and research gaze? Read here

Conserving Freshwater Ecosystems in India: A Call to Action

This paper calls for an urgent and greater focus on implementing conservation actions for freshwater ecosystems in India and suggests a strategy to enhance focus on their conservation. Read here
Convenience over Control: Qualitative Insights from Water System Users in a Rural Setting in Gujarat, India.

This study suggests that piped water system designs should enable operational flexibility, tailored to community needs, so that water is available when needed. Read here
Disputes, (de)Politicization and Democracy: Interstate Water Disputes in India

The aleatory nature of politics reshapes the nature and extent of a dispute and contributes to its frequent recurrence. Discourses of policy and governance reforms usually do not account for this contingent nature of politics. Read here
Water Disputes and the Environment: Transboundary Dimensions

This chapter analyses India’s transboundary water relationships, arguing that despite its hydrohegemonic tendencies and preference for bilateralism; shared environmental risks in South Asia create an opportunity to build regional institutions, starting with disaster resilience as a foundation for cooperation. Read here
The Human Right to Water in Rural India – Promises and Challenges

India has made remarkable progress in rural drinking water access, rising from 18 percent coverage in 1974 to at least 72 percent today. While this reflects significant advancement in realising the human right to water, full and universal access remains an ongoing challenge. Read here

The Right to Water in Rural India and Drinking Water Policy Reforms

This chapter uncovers the role played by the state in providing significant resources,like water, to all in rural India. It further analyses the changes that have taken place and the gaps that have arisen in terms of aligning the policy framework with the human right to water.
Read here

Whither India’s Federal Governance for Long-Term Water Security?

The discourse about federal governance is generally dominated by that of fiscal federalism. This chapter takes a closer look at the historical changes in budgetary allocations of the Centre and select states for water resources governance, and argues that federal water governance in India is weakly structured to pursue its development and sustainability goals. Read here

Shifting Scales from International to Subnational: A Comparative Analysis of India and Germany’s Federal Water Governance

This paper examines the River Basin Management trajectory of Germany vis-à-vis India through a comparative lens. It argues for acknowledging structural differences to enable meaningful knowledge exchanges and  collaborations at the sub-national scale. Read here

Unravelling Rural India’s enduring water indigence: framing the questions, issues, options and opportunities

The paper extensively reviews India’s centrally sponsored programme for improving drinking water supply coverage in rural settlements. Read here
India should take a leaf out of Singapore’s water harvesting to solve its crisis

How have India’s collaborative arrangements with Singapore fared? Read here
